cur:manuscripts-rossano-christ-barabbas.summary: In an apse-like semicircle, Pilate sits enthroned behind a table flanked by imperial standards, surrounded by the crowd who cry out. In the lower register Christ stands calm and haloed among guards, while on the right the bound Barabbas is held by his captors. The page shows the decisive moment of the trial, when the people choose Barabbas over Christ.
facts: Unusually, the Rossano artist did not show the familiar hand-washing of Pilate but the opening of the trial and the choice between Christ and Barabbas, as discussed in the Wikipedia account of the manuscript.
Pilate's commanding position, with Christ lower and to one side, distinguishes these two trial pages from most later versions of the scene.

feat:barlach-das-wiedersehen.summary: Two long-robed figures meet in an embrace: the risen Christ, thin and upright, supports the doubting apostle Thomas, who sinks against him and gazes up into his face. Barlach reduces the Gospel encounter to two bodies and one gesture of recognition and mercy. It is one of the most tender works of German Expressionist sculpture.
facts: Barlach, also a playwright, was preoccupied with themes of doubt, longing and spiritual rebirth, which this sculpture embodies.

The wooden original was bought by the Schwerin state museum soon after it was carved, but was confiscated by the Nazis as 'degenerate art' in 1937; it later passed to the Hamburg collector Hermann F. Reemtsma.

Bronze casts of the group are in several collections, including the Osthaus Museum in Hagen and the Laurentiuskirche in Herne-Wanne, so that Barlach's image of doubt and recognition can still be seen in churches and museums across Germany.
